name: Weekly Reality Check Journal
description: A maintenance exercise for healthy thinkers. A weekly self-check to spot any creeping cognitive distortions before they grow into patterns.
research_basis: CBT metacognition maintenance protocols
tutorial_steps: Once a week, write about one situation that bothered you.
Ask: Was my thinking accurate? Did I catastrophize, overgeneralize, or mind-read?
If yes: write a more balanced version.
If your thinking was accurate: note how you handled it well.
End with one thing you're proud of this week.
tips: This is a tune-up, not a repair. Brief and light — the goal is awareness, not deep analysis.
video_title: Journaling for Cognitive Awareness (YouTube)

name: Daily Thought Awareness
goals: Notice thinking patterns before they cause distress
description: A brief daily awareness practice — just noticing thoughts without reacting to them. Builds the foundational skill that makes all CBT exercises more effective.
research_basis: CBT metacognition (Wells, 2000); Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT)
tutorial_steps: Once a day, pause for 2-3 minutes and observe your current thoughts.
Don't judge them — just notice: What am I thinking? Is this thought helpful? Is it accurate?
You don't need to change anything. Just observe.
If you notice a distorted thought: acknowledge it ('There's that all-or-nothing thinking again') and move on.
tips: Noticing a thought and being ruled by it are two different things. This exercise builds the distance between them.
video_title: How to Observe Your Thoughts — Mindfulness & CBT (YouTube)

name: Simplified Thought Record
description: A beginner-friendly CBT thought record. Focuses on 3 steps: noticing the thought, naming the distortion, writing one more balanced counter-thought.
research_basis: Beck CBT simplified protocols; CBT self-help research
tutorial_steps: When you notice a strong negative feeling, write down the thought causing it.
Name the type of distortion: All-or-nothing / Catastrophizing / Mind reading / Overgeneralization / Self-labeling / Should statements.
Write ONE more balanced alternative thought — not positive, just more realistic.
Example: Thought: 'I always mess everything up.' Type: Overgeneralization. Balanced: 'I made a mistake today, but I've handled many things well this week.'
tips: You don't have to eliminate the distorted thought — just create a crack in its certainty.
video_title: CBT Thought Record — Beginners Guide (YouTube)

name: Challenge Questions for Negative Thoughts
frequency: Whenever a strong negative thought appears
description: A set of Socratic questions from CBT that challenge automatic negative thoughts by examining their validity, usefulness, and alternatives.
research_basis: Socratic questioning in CBT (Beck, 1979); Cognitive restructuring
tutorial_steps: When a negative thought arises, run it through these questions:
1. Is this thought based on facts or feelings?
2. What is the actual evidence FOR this thought?
3. What is the evidence AGAINST it?
4. What would I tell my best friend if they had this thought?
5. What's the most realistic outcome — not worst, not best?
6. Is this thought helpful to me right now?
Write brief answers or go through mentally.
tips: The questions work best when written out at least the first few times.
video_title: Challenging Negative Thoughts — CBT Techniques (YouTube)

name: Balanced Thinking Practice
description: A daily practice of deliberately generating balanced perspectives alongside negative ones — training the brain to default toward nuanced thinking.
research_basis: CBT cognitive restructuring; Cognitive flexibility research
tutorial_steps: Once a day, identify one situation you've been thinking about negatively.
Write the negative thought first — honestly.
Then write an equally plausible positive or neutral interpretation.
Then write the balanced view: 'The truth is probably somewhere between these two.'
Practice holding both perspectives in mind simultaneously.
tips: Balanced thinking is not toxic positivity. It acknowledges the negative AND includes what the negative view is missing.
video_title: Balanced Thinking — CBT Core Skill (YouTube)

name: Daily Full Thought Record
description: The full CBT thought record applied daily for moderate-severe cognitive distortions. Consistent daily use creates measurable change within 3-6 weeks.
research_basis: Beck (1979); CBT efficacy for cognitive distortions; NICE guidelines
tutorial_steps: SITUATION: What happened? Where, when, who was involved?
AUTOMATIC THOUGHT: Write the exact thought.
DISTORTION TYPE: Label it (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing, mind reading, etc.)
EMOTION: Name and rate 0-100.
EVIDENCE FOR: Facts that support the thought.
EVIDENCE AGAINST: Facts that challenge it.
BALANCED THOUGHT: A realistic alternative acknowledging both sides.
RE-RATE EMOTION: What's the intensity now?
Do this daily for minimum 3 weeks. Change is cumulative.
tips: The first week feels mechanical. By week 3, the questioning becomes automatic. Consistency is the mechanism.
video_title: Full CBT Thought Record — Daily Practice (YouTube)

name: Evidence For & Against
goals: Test the reality of a feared or negative belief
description: A targeted CBT exercise examining a specific feared belief by rigorously listing factual evidence on both sides — like being your own defense attorney.
research_basis: Beck CBT Dysfunctional Thought Record; Evidence-based cognitive restructuring
tutorial_steps: Write the feared belief as a specific statement (e.g., 'If I fail this presentation, my career is over.').
Column A — Evidence FOR: List only facts (not feelings) that support this belief.
Column B — Evidence AGAINST: List facts that contradict or complicate this belief. Include past exceptions and others' perspectives.
Rate belief strength before and after (0-100%).
Write a balanced conclusion that integrates both columns.
tips: 'I feel like a failure' is not evidence. 'I received negative feedback on two projects' is. Only facts go in the FOR column.
video_title: Evidence For and Against — CBT Technique (YouTube)

name: Reality Testing
goals: Test distorted beliefs against real-world evidence
description: A behavioral experiment where you test whether distorted beliefs are actually true by collecting real evidence — moving from thinking to testing.
research_basis: CBT behavioral experiments (Bennett-Levy et al., 2004)
tutorial_steps: Identify a belief you hold strongly (e.g., 'Everyone thinks I'm incompetent at work').
Design a small test: what evidence could you collect? (e.g., 'I'll notice how people respond to my next 5 contributions in meetings')
Collect evidence over 3-7 days. Write it down.
Review: does real-world evidence support or contradict the belief?
Update the belief based on evidence, not feeling.
tips: Cognitive distortions survive because we never test them. Behavioral testing uses real data.
video_title: CBT Behavioral Experiments — Testing Your Beliefs (YouTube)

name: Intensive Thought Tracking
description: For severe cognitive distortions, intensive tracking of every significant negative thought throughout the day maps the full pattern for targeted professional CBT work.
research_basis: CBT severe distortion protocols; Thought monitoring in CBT-D and CBT-A
tutorial_steps: Keep a note available throughout the day.
Every time you have a significant negative thought, log it: time, trigger, thought, distortion type, emotion 0-100.
At end of each day: review all entries. Which distortion type comes up most?
Bring your tracking log to sessions with a professional if you have one.
After 2 weeks: identify your 2-3 most frequent distortion patterns. These are your targets.
tips: Severity at this level warrants professional CBT alongside self-help. Use this tracking to support professional work.
video_title: Intensive Thought Monitoring for CBT (YouTube)

name: Find a CBT Professional
goals: Access professional CBT for severe distortions
description: Severe cognitive distortions have a strong evidence base for professional CBT treatment. Self-help can support but not replace structured CBT at this level.
research_basis: NICE guidelines for CBT; CBT efficacy meta-analysis (Butler et al., 2006)
tutorial_steps: Search for a therapist specifically trained in CBT.
Ask directly: 'Do you use CBT? Do you have experience with cognitive distortions?'
For online options: look for platforms that match with CBT-trained therapists.
Take your thought tracking log to the first session.
Commit to at least 8-12 sessions before assessing effectiveness.
tips: For severe cognitive distortions, CBT has strong evidence of effectiveness.
video_title: What is CBT and How to Find a CBT Therapist (YouTube)

name: Cognitive Distortion Log
description: A structured daily log organized by distortion type, designed to reveal patterns and track change over time in severe cognitive distortion.
research_basis: CBT dysfunctional thought diary; Beck Cognitive Distortions taxonomy
tutorial_steps: Keep a table: Date, Thought, Distortion Type, Emotion before (0-100), Balanced thought, Emotion after (0-100).
Fill in at least one row per day.
Weekly: count how many of each distortion type appeared. Which is most frequent?
Focus your challenging efforts on your most frequent type.
Track emotion before/after scores over weeks — improvement shows up in these numbers.
tips: The distortion log turns an abstract problem into concrete, trackable data. That data is what makes change measurable.
video_title: Cognitive Distortion Log — How to Track Thinking Patterns (YouTube)

name: Complete Your First Check-In
description: The hardest step is the first one. Completing one check-in now starts the engagement loop and gives you real data about yourself.
research_basis: Habit formation; Behavioral initiation research
tutorial_steps: Open the app right now.
Complete today's mood and wellbeing check-in — it takes 2 minutes.
Read your results.
That's it — you just completed your first step.
tips: You don't need to feel ready. Just do the 2-minute check-in. Everything else follows.

name: Try One Exercise Today
description: Trying one exercise — even briefly — shifts the experience from passive to active and increases the likelihood of return.
research_basis: Behavioral activation; App engagement research
tutorial_steps: Choose any exercise from your suggested list.
Do it now — don't wait for the 'right time'.
Rate how you feel before and after on 1-10.
You just completed one full cycle. You know this tool works.
tips: The 'right time' is a myth. Starting any time is the right time.

name: Set an App Reminder
goals: Use external cue to build habit
description: External reminders are one of the most effective habit-formation tools. Setting a daily reminder removes the memory burden and creates a consistent cue.
research_basis: Habit formation (Duhigg, 2012); Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999)
tutorial_steps: Set a daily phone alarm for a consistent time — ideally morning or evening.
Label it something motivating: 'Mentora — 5 mins for me'.
When it goes off: open the app immediately and complete a check-in.
Don't dismiss and delay — that defeats the habit loop.
tips: Attaching the check-in to an existing daily habit (coffee, brushing teeth) makes it even more reliable.

name: Set Your Daily Routine
goals: Transition from sporadic to habitual use
description: Moving from occasional to daily use requires a simple, consistent routine.
research_basis: Habit loop (cue-routine-reward); Consistency in digital mental health tools
tutorial_steps: Choose a specific time for your daily check-in (e.g., 8 AM, or 9 PM).
Decide the context: in bed, at your desk, with coffee.
Set a recurring alarm for this time.
Commit to 7 consecutive days. After 7 days: has it become more automatic?
tips: Same time + same place = fastest habit formation. The context itself becomes the cue.

name: 5-Day Exercise Challenge
description: A structured 5-day challenge to build the habit of completing daily exercises. Short, defined challenges are highly effective for habit initiation.
research_basis: Habit formation short challenge structures; Behavioral Activation
tutorial_steps: Choose one exercise type to focus on for 5 days (e.g., breathing, journaling, or CBT).
Do it every day for 5 days at the same time.
Track completion each day — even just a checkmark.
At end of day 5: how did it feel? Did it get easier?
If yes: extend to 7 days, then 14.
tips: 5 days is short enough to commit to, long enough to feel the benefit.

name: Build a 3-Day Streak
description: A 3-day streak goal is concrete, achievable, and motivating. Short streak goals build the consistency muscle.
research_basis: Gamification and habit formation; Short-goal commitment research
tutorial_steps: Set a goal: 3 consecutive days of check-ins and at least one exercise each day.
Each day: open the app, complete check-in, do one exercise.
After day 3: celebrate. Then set a new goal of 7 days.
If you miss a day: restart the 3-day count from the next day. Never quit — just restart.
tips: Missing once doesn't break a habit. Missing twice starts to. The rule is: never miss twice.

name: Celebrate Your Progress
description: Recognizing and celebrating progress is one of the most evidence-based ways to sustain long-term behavior change.
research_basis: Self-Determination Theory; Positive reinforcement; Progress principle (Amabile & Kramer)
tutorial_steps: Once a week, take 5 minutes to review your week.
Write: What did I actually do this week? (exercises completed, check-ins, insights)
Write: What difference did I notice? Even small ones count.
Acknowledge the effort: 'I showed up for myself this week. That matters.'
Set one intention for next week.
tips: Progress feels invisible when you don't track it. This reflection makes progress visible — which is what sustains motivation.

name: Build a 14-Day Streak
goals: Solidify daily engagement as a habit
description: 14 days of consistent daily practice crosses the initial habit formation threshold.
research_basis: Habit automaticity research (Lally et al., 2010); Self-Determination Theory
tutorial_steps: Commit to 14 consecutive days of daily check-in + one exercise.
Track each day. Protect the streak.
On day 7: how is it feeling vs. day 1?
On day 14: what's changed? What feels more automatic?
tips: The goal is automaticity — the feeling that checking in requires less conscious effort. That's the habit forming.

name: Weekly Reflection
description: Regular structured reflection consolidates learning and identifies patterns, making the self-help work progressively more effective.
research_basis: Reflective practice research; Kolb learning cycle; CBT session review
tutorial_steps: At the end of each week, write answers to:
1. What exercises did I do? Which felt most useful?
2. What did I notice about my mood/anxiety/stress this week?
3. What pattern am I seeing?
4. What do I want to focus on next week?
Keep it under 10 minutes.
tips: Reflection turns experience into learning. Without it, you practice but don't progress.

name: Acknowledge Your Dedication
description: For users with excellent engagement, acknowledging dedication deepens intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy.
research_basis: Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan); Intrinsic motivation and sustained behavior
tutorial_steps: Take 5 minutes to write about your journey: where you started, what's different now.
Be specific about what you've done and what it cost you in effort.
Acknowledge that consistently showing up for your mental health is not trivial.
Write: 'I am someone who takes care of my mental health. This is part of who I am.'
tips: Identity-based reinforcement ('I am the kind of person who...') is more powerful for long-term behavior than reward-based reinforcement.

name: Deep Monthly Reflection
goals: Extract maximum insight from sustained practice
description: For highly engaged users, a monthly deep reflection session extracts the most from sustained practice.
research_basis: Reflective practice; CBT case conceptualization self-application
tutorial_steps: Review the past month's data: scores, exercises, patterns.
Write: What has genuinely changed? What hasn't changed yet? What do I understand about myself now that I didn't before?
Identify: What is my biggest remaining challenge area?
Set one specific goal for next month with a concrete plan.
Write: What kind of mental health do I want in 3 months, and what will get me there?
tips: Month-level reflection reveals gradual changes that are only visible when you look at the longer arc.

name: Share Your Progress
description: Sharing progress with trusted others reinforces commitment through social accountability.
research_basis: Social accountability in behavior change; Narrative identity research
tutorial_steps: Think of one meaningful change or insight from your mental health work.
Share it with one person you trust — a friend, family member, or community.
You don't have to share everything — just one real thing that's changed.
Notice how sharing it affects your own relationship to the progress.
tips: Naming our progress out loud makes it more real and more lasting.

name: Continue Normal Coping
goals: Maintain emotional safety through regular coping
description: No crisis indicators present. Continue regular wellbeing practices and daily check-ins.
research_basis: C-SSRS safety confirmation protocols
tutorial_steps: Continue your regular exercises and check-ins.
If anything changes in how you feel, the app's check-in will catch it.
It's always okay to talk to someone you trust about how you're feeling.
tips: Regular check-ins are what catch changes early — before they become crises.

name: Everyday Coping Toolkit
description: Building a personal toolkit of coping strategies that work for you — before a crisis — is one of the most protective things you can do.
research_basis: Resilience research; Proactive coping; Crisis prevention
tutorial_steps: Write a list of 5-7 things that help you feel better when you're having a hard day.
Include physical (walk, shower, food), social (call someone), and mental (journaling, breathing).
Rate each 1-5 for how well they work.
Save this list where you can find it easily.
Next time you're struggling: go to the list FIRST before defaulting to unhelpful coping.
tips: The best coping strategies are the ones YOU know work for you specifically.

name: Identify Your Support Network
goals: Map available support before it's needed urgently
description: When feeling passive distress or pain, mapping your support network is the most important protective step.
research_basis: Safety planning research; Social support and suicide prevention
tutorial_steps: Write the names of people in your life you could reach out to if struggling.
Include: one family member, one friend, one professional contact if available.
For each: what would you say? How would you reach them?
Also write: what is one thing I can do for myself when I'm struggling?
Keep this list accessible.
tips: Knowing your supports before you need them means you don't have to figure it out at your lowest.
video_title: Building Your Support Network (YouTube)

name: Talk to Someone You Trust
description: When experiencing passive suicidal thoughts or intense pain, talking to a trusted person is the most evidence-based protective action.
research_basis: Crisis intervention; Social support and suicide prevention research
tutorial_steps: Identify one person you trust.
Contact them today: 'I've been having a really hard time and I needed to talk to someone.'
Let them respond. Let them support you.
If talking feels too hard: text. If texting feels too hard: call.
If there is no one: contact a support line. findahelpline.com has options by country.
tips: Keeping pain completely private increases risk. Breaking the silence — even once, with one person — is protective.
video_title: How to Talk About Suicidal Thoughts (YouTube)

name: Reach Out to a Professional
goals: Connect to professional mental health support
description: Passive suicidal thoughts or intense emotional pain warrant professional support. This is the appropriate level of care.
research_basis: C-SSRS passive ideation protocol; SAFE-T assessment
tutorial_steps: Contact your doctor, therapist, or mental health line today.
Tell them honestly what you've been experiencing.
If you don't have a therapist: ask your doctor for a referral or call a mental health line.
Egypt: 08008880700. International: findahelpline.com
You don't have to be 'bad enough' to deserve professional support.
tips: Seeking professional help at this stage is prevention, not crisis response.
video_title: How to Seek Mental Health Help (YouTube)

name: Seek Professional Help Urgently
goals: Urgent connection to mental health professional
description: Active thoughts of death or self-harm require immediate professional support. This is a medical situation.
research_basis: C-SSRS moderate risk protocol; Crisis intervention
tutorial_steps: Contact a mental health professional today — not this week, today.
If you have a therapist: contact them now and describe your current thoughts.
If you don't: go to the nearest hospital emergency department or call a crisis line.
Egypt: 08008880700. International: findahelpline.com
Tell someone you trust what you're experiencing and ask them to stay with you or check in.
tips: These thoughts deserve immediate professional attention. You are not a burden. You deserve this support.
video_title: Crisis Support Resources (YouTube)

name: Detailed Safety Plan
description: A detailed written safety plan for moderate-to-high risk. The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention has strong evidence for reducing suicide risk.
research_basis: Stanley & Brown (2012) Safety Planning Intervention; SAFE-T protocol; C-SSRS
tutorial_steps: WARNING SIGNS: What thoughts, feelings, or situations signal a crisis is building?
INTERNAL COPING: 3 things you can do ALONE to reduce distress right now.
PEOPLE/PLACES: 2-3 people or places to be around others — just to not be alone.
TRUSTED PEOPLE: 2 people you can tell when you're in crisis. Names and how to reach them.
PROFESSIONALS: Therapist name and number. Crisis line number.
MEANS REDUCTION: Is there anything at home that could be used to hurt yourself? Plan to reduce your access to it.
Print this or save it where you can find it in a crisis.
tips: Build this with the help of a professional if possible. Reviewed safety plans are more effective than ones built alone.
video_title: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (YouTube)

name: Immediate Crisis Action
description: Immediate danger requires immediate action. Your safety is the only priority right now.
research_basis: Crisis intervention; Emergency mental health protocols
tutorial_steps: Call emergency services in your country RIGHT NOW (Egypt: 123 police, or go to nearest hospital).
Or call a crisis line: Egypt 08008880700. International: findahelpline.com
If possible: go to someone you trust immediately and ask them to stay with you.
If you have access to means: put distance between yourself and them right now.
You are worth saving. Help is available.
tips: This is a medical emergency. Please reach out to emergency services or crisis support right now.
video_title: Crisis Helpline — How to Get Immediate Help (YouTube)

name: Emergency Services
goals: Access emergency mental health support immediately
description: Emergency contacts for immediate mental health crisis.
research_basis: Crisis intervention protocol
tutorial_steps: Egypt emergency: Call 123 (police) or go to nearest hospital emergency department.
Egypt mental health line: 08008880700
International crisis lines: findahelpline.com
If you cannot call: text a crisis line where available.
If you are with someone: show them this screen and ask for help.
tips: You do not have to be 'certain' to call. Feeling unsafe is enough reason.
video_title: Emergency Mental Health Resources (YouTube)

name: Ask Someone to Stay With You
goals: Immediate human presence as protective factor
description: Human presence is one of the most protective factors in acute crisis. Asking someone to be with you is a direct safety action.
research_basis: Crisis intervention; Means restriction and presence as protective factors
tutorial_steps: Text or call the person closest to you right now.
Say: 'I'm having a really hard time and I need someone to be with me.'
You don't have to explain everything. Just ask them to come or stay on the phone.
If no one is reachable: go to a public place or a hospital. Not alone.
tips: Asking for presence is not dramatic or a burden. It is the right thing to do right now.
video_title: How to Ask for Help in a Crisis (YouTube)

name: Reduce Access to Means
goals: Direct risk reduction through means restriction
description: Means restriction is one of the most evidence-based suicide prevention interventions. Creating distance between yourself and potential means saves lives.
research_basis: Means restriction and suicide prevention (Mann et al., 2005); SAFE-T means restriction protocol
tutorial_steps: Think about what you might use to hurt yourself.
Remove it from your immediate environment right now — give it to someone, lock it away, leave it elsewhere.
Ask someone you trust to hold onto it: 'Can you hold onto this for me for a while?'
You don't have to explain why.
Even one step of distance creates time — and time is what makes crisis survivable.
tips: Most suicide attempts happen impulsively. Means restriction extends the time between impulse and access — and that time is life-saving.
video_title: Means Restriction — A Life-Saving Intervention (YouTube)
